claim: The vertebrate gastrointestinal tract harbors the highest density of microbes recorded for any microbial habitat.
source: The vertebrate gastrointestinal tract harbors the highest density of microbes recorded for any microbial habitat (Whitman et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Whitman et al., 1998

claim: Microbial communities in the gastrointestinal tract are required for normal host development and physiology.
source: These microbial communities are not only tolerated by their hosts, but are also required for normal host development and physiology, highlighting the intimacy of these mutualisms (McFall-Ngai et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to McFall-Ngai et al., 2013

claim: Excessive inflammation is associated with inflammatory bowel disease, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and sepsis.
source: This knowledge is critical to dissect the microbial etiology of a range of diseases associated with excessive inflammation, including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and sepsis (Huttenhower et al., 2014; Turnbaugh et al., 2006; Wen et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huttenhower et al., 2014; Turnbaugh et al., 2006; Wen et al., 2008

claim: Bacteroidetes fragilis produces a zwitterionic polysaccharide PSA that induces a toleragenic T cell profile and protects against intestinal inflammation.
source: One such factor is the zwitterionic polysaccharide, PSA, produced by the human symbiont Bacteroidetes fragilis, that induces a toleragenic T cell profile and protects against intestinal inflammation (Mazmanian et al., 2008; Mazmanian et al., 2005; Round and Mazmanian, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mazmanian et al., 2008; Mazmanian et al., 2005; Round and Mazmanian, 2010

claim: Lactobacillus rhamnosus secretes anti-inflammatory proteins p75 and p40.
source: The anti-inflammatory properties of Lactobacillus rhamnosus have been attributed to secreted proteins p75 and p40 (Yan et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yan et al., 2007

claim: Faecalibacterium prausnitzii secretes an anti-inflammatory 15 kDa protein called microbial anti-inflammatory molecule (MAM).
source: Faecalibacterium prausnitzii secretes an anti-inflammatory 15 kDa protein called microbial anti-inflammatory molecule or MAM (Yan et al., 2007; Quévrain et al., 2016; Sokol et al., 2008; Carlsson et al., 2013; Martín et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yan et al., 2007; Quévrain et al., 2016; Sokol et al., 2008; Carlsson et al., 2013; Martín et al., 2014

claim: Secreted proteins from Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii reduce inflammation in mouse models of colitis.
source: These secreted proteins reduce inflammation in mouse models of colitis (Yan et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yan et al., 2011

claim: Zebrafish embryos develop ex-utero within their protective chorions.
source: Zebrafish embryos develop ex-utero within their protective chorions and first encounter environmental microbes when they hatch as larvae between 2 and 3 days post fertilization (dpf).
evidence: Stated as a fact about zebrafish development

claim: Zebrafish larvae have a fully functional digestive tract that is colonized with bacteria by 5 dpf.
source: By 5 dpf the animals have a fully functional digestive tract that is colonized with bacteria (Bates et al., 2006; Stephens et al., 2016; Wallace et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bates et al., 2006; Stephens et al., 2016; Wallace et al., 2005

claim: Zebrafish larvae have a functional innate immune system with neutrophils and macrophages before adaptive immune cells emerge at approximately 3 weeks of age.
source: The larvae are also equipped with a functional innate immune system with highly dynamic neutrophils and macrophages that serve as the primary cellular defenses before the emergence of adaptive immune cells at approximately 3 weeks of age (Renshaw and Trede, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Renshaw and Trede, 2012

claim: Intestinal neutrophil populations in larval zebrafish average 3 cells in germ free animals and 7 cells in conventionally reared animals.
source: For example, we have shown that intestinal neutrophil populations in larval zebrafish range from an average of 3 cells in germ free (GF) animals to 7 cells in conventionally reared (CV) animals, a difference that can be readily detected in well-powered experiments despite extensive inter-host variation (Rolig et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rolig et al., 2015

claim: Aeromonas is the sole bacterial genus present in 100% of zebrafish individuals at all developmental time points.
source: Aeromonas is an important symbiont of the zebrafish and the sole bacterial genus that we found present in 100% of individuals at all developmental time points in a comprehensive longitudinal study of zebrafish gut microbiomes across their lifespan (Stephens et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stephens et al., 2016

claim: Aeromonas can fully rescue defects in glycan expression in germ-free zebrafish.
source: Furthermore, we have shown that in mono-associations, representatives of the Aeromonas genus can fully rescue defects in glycan expression (Bates et al., 2006), epithelial cell proliferation (Cheesman et al., 2011), innate immune response (Rolig et al., 2015), and pancreatic beta cell expansion (Hill et al., 2016) that are characteristic phenotypes of GF fish.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bates et al., 2006

claim: Aeromonas can fully rescue defects in epithelial cell proliferation in germ-free zebrafish.
source: Furthermore, we have shown that in mono-associations, representatives of the Aeromonas genus can fully rescue defects in glycan expression (Bates et al., 2006), epithelial cell proliferation (Cheesman et al., 2011), innate immune response (Rolig et al., 2015), and pancreatic beta cell expansion (Hill et al., 2016) that are characteristic phenotypes of GF fish.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cheesman et al., 2011

claim: Aeromonas can fully rescue defects in innate immune response in germ-free zebrafish.
source: Furthermore, we have shown that in mono-associations, representatives of the Aeromonas genus can fully rescue defects in glycan expression (Bates et al., 2006), epithelial cell proliferation (Cheesman et al., 2011), innate immune response (Rolig et al., 2015), and pancreatic beta cell expansion (Hill et al., 2016) that are characteristic phenotypes of GF fish.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rolig et al., 2015

claim: Aeromonas can fully rescue defects in pancreatic beta cell expansion in germ-free zebrafish.
source: Furthermore, we have shown that in mono-associations, representatives of the Aeromonas genus can fully rescue defects in glycan expression (Bates et al., 2006), epithelial cell proliferation (Cheesman et al., 2011), innate immune response (Rolig et al., 2015), and pancreatic beta cell expansion (Hill et al., 2016) that are characteristic phenotypes of GF fish.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hill et al., 2016

claim: Neutrophils are responsive to both infecting pathogens and resident intestinal microbes.
source: Neutrophils are a primary component of the initial inflammatory response and are responsive to both infecting pathogens and resident intestinal microbes (Harvie and Huttenlocher, 2015; Bates et al., 2007; Kanther et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harvie and Huttenlocher, 2015; Bates et al., 2007; Kanther et al., 2014

claim: The ΔT2 mutant of A. veronii strain Hm21 induced a greater intestinal neutrophil response than the ΔT2C complemented strain.
source: The ΔT2C and ΔT2 colonized the zebrafish intestine to similar levels in mono-associations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), however the ΔT2 mutant induced a greater intestinal neutrophil response than the ΔT2C (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: A. veronii strain Hm21 secretes a product that decreases the neutrophil response to its colonization.
source: This result suggests that A. veronii strain Hm21 secretes a product that decreases the neutrophil response to its colonization.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ΔT2 mutant induced greater neutrophil response than ΔT2C

claim: The increased neutrophil response to ΔT2 was rescued by concurrent treatment with cell-free supernatant from the ΔT2C strain.
source: The increased neutrophil response to ΔT2 was rescued by concurrent treatment with cell-free supernatant (CFS) collected from the ΔT2C strain, but not CFS collected from ΔT2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Mass-spectrophotometry identified 22 proteins enriched by greater than 10 counts in the ΔT2C CFS compared to the ΔT2 strain.
source: This analysis resulted in a list of 22 proteins that were enriched by greater than 10 counts in the ΔT2C CFS (Supplemental file 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Supplemental file 1

claim: Neutrophil modulating activity was found primarily in the 40–60% ammonium sulfate fraction of ΔT2C CFS.
source: We found neutrophil modulating activity primarily in the 40–60% salt fraction, but also saw some activity in the 20–40% salt fraction (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The 33 kDa uncharacterized protein (UP) modulated the neutrophil response to ΔT2 colonization.
source: We treated zebrafish mono-associated with ΔT2 with the CFS resulting from overexpression of each protein of interest and found neutrophil modulating activity in the E. coli CFS with the 33 kDa UP and not with CBP or control CFS from E. coli containing an empty expression vector (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The neutrophil-modulating protein was named Aeromonas immune modulator A (AimA).
source: We named this neutrophil-modulating protein Aeromonas immune modulator A (AimA).
evidence: Authors' naming decision based on protein function

claim: No homologues to AimA exist outside of the Aeromonas genera based on DNA and amino acid homology searches.
source: DNA and amino acid homology searches revealed that no homologues to AimA exist outside of the Aeromonas genera.
evidence: Based on bioinformatic sequence analysis

claim: The molecular structure of AimA was determined to a resolution of 2.3 Å using SAD phasing.
source: We determined the molecular structure of AimA using a heavy atom derivative and Single-wavelength Anomalous Dispersion (SAD) phasing to a resolution of 2.3 Å (PDB 6B7L; Table 2).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data in Table 2 and PDB deposition 6B7L

claim: The structure of AimA revealed two domains connected by a short linker.
source: The structure of AimA revealed two domains connected by a short linker (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 2A,B

claim: Both domains of AimA have similarity to proteins in the calycin superfamily.
source: Therefore, we performed structural homology searches against each domain separately, which revealed that both domains had similarity to proteins in the calycin superfamily (Supplemental file 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural homology search results in Supplemental file 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The N-term domain of AimA has structural homology to streptavidin.
source: The N-term domain of AimA has an incomplete β-barrel, but maintains some structural homology to streptavidin.
evidence: Based on structural comparison analysis

claim: AimA does not bind biotin.
source: Streptavidin binds biotin tightly, but we found no evidence that AimA binds biotin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The C-term domain of AimA has structural homology to avidins and lipocalins.
source: The C-term domain of AimA has structural homology both to avidins and lipocalins (Supplemental file 2).
evidence: Supported by structural homology search results in Supplemental file 2

claim: Feeding zebrafish 0.3% soysaponin from 4 dpf to 6 dpf significantly increased the number of intestinal neutrophils.
source: We fed conventionally raised zebrafish larvae Zeiglers fish food with 0.3% soysaponin from 4 dpf to 6 dpf and saw a significant increase in the number of intestinal neutrophils in response to the soysaponin, as expected (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Treatment with 100 ng/mL purified AimA prevented the increase in neutrophil influx in response to soysaponin.
source: When we treated the fish with 100 ng/mL purified AimA concurrently with soysaponin, AimA prevented the increase in neutrophil influx in response to soysaponin (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: AimA can inhibit pro-inflammatory signaling pathways elicited by stimuli other than Aeromonas.
source: This result demonstrates that AimA alone can inhibit pro-inflammatory signaling pathways elicited by stimuli other than Aeromonas.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AimA prevents soysaponin-induced inflammation

claim: The C-term domain of AimA overlaps structurally with the SCR1 of mouse lipocalin-2.
source: The SCR1 in the C-term domain of AimA overlaps structurally with the SCR1 of mouse lipocalin-2 (mLCN2) and shares some related amino acids (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3B

claim: Addition of mLCN2 concurrently with soysaponin did not influence the neutrophil response to soysaponin.
source: We found that the addition of mLCN2 concurrently with soysaponin did not influence the neutrophil response to soysaponin (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Addition of mLCN2 in conjunction with AimA blocked the protective effect of AimA against soysaponin-induced inflammation.
source: however, addition of mLCN2 in conjunction with AimA blocked the protective effect of AimA against soysaponin-induced inflammation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: mLCN2 may interfere with AimA's activity by direct binding, competing for the same host receptor, or acting in a competing pathway.
source: This result suggests that mLCN2 may interfere with AimA's activity by direct binding, competing for the same host receptor, or acting in a competing pathway.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental results

claim: LCN2's immunomodulatory activity is mediated by binding iron-sequestering siderophores, including enterobactin from E. coli.
source: LCN2's immunomodulatory activity is mediated, at least in part, by binding iron-sequestering siderophores, including enterobactin from E. coli (Xiao et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Xiao et al., 2017

claim: The homologous regions of the N- and C-term domains of AimA are much narrower than the enterobactin-binding cleft of LCN2.
source: However, in comparison to the wide enterobactin-binding cleft (calyx) of LCN2, the homologous regions of the N- and C-term domains of AimA are much narrower, are occluded by loops or a helix, and lack the enterobactin-interacting residues of LCN (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–F

claim: AimA does not inhibit E. coli K12 growth under iron limiting conditions.
source: In contrast, when we added the same range of concentrations of purified AimA protein to the E. coli cultures, we saw no growth inhibition (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that AimA does not bind and sequester enterobactin in a similar manner to LCN2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G

claim: Both the N- and C-term domains of AimA alone were sufficient to reduce the neutrophil response in the soysaponin model of intestinal inflammation.
source: We found that both the N- and C-term domains alone were sufficient to reduce the neutrophil response in the soysaponin model of intestinal inflammation (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The N- and C-term domains of AimA share only 17% amino acid identity.
source: Although they share only 17% amino acid identity, a structural overlay between the two domains reveals some structural conservation (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by sequence and structural analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: An almost identical homologue (99%) to AimA exists in zebrafish intestinal Aeromonas isolate ZOR0001.
source: We found an almost identical homologue (99%) to AimA in a zebrafish intestinal Aeromonas isolate, ZOR0001, referred to here as ZF Aer (Table 1) (Stephens et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and citation to Stephens et al., 2016

claim: Some Aeromonas species have both AimA and a second copy named AimB.
source: Some Aeromonas species, including A. veronii strain Hm21 (Table 1), have both AimA and a second copy, which we named AimB.
evidence: Based on genomic analysis

claim: AimB is distantly related to AimA by amino acid sequence conservation (27%).
source: AimB is distantly related to AimA by amino acid sequence conservation (27%), yet a model generated by the Iterative Threading ASSEmbly Refinement (I-TASSER) program of the structure of AimB overlays directly on the structure of AimA (Figure 5A) (Yang et al., 2015; Roy et al., 2010; Zhang, 2008).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and structural modeling shown in Figure 5A, with citations to Yang et al., 2015; Roy et al., 2010; Zhang, 2008

claim: ZF Aer ΔaimA mutant colonized gnotobiotic zebrafish to lower levels than its wild type counterpart.
source: We found that when inoculated into GF larvae at 3 dpf, the ZF Aer ΔaimA mutant colonized gnotobiotic zebrafish to lower levels than its wild type counterpart (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The colonization defect of ZF Aer ΔaimA became apparent at 7 dpf.
source: with the colonization defect becoming apparent at 7 dpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: The Aer ΔAΔB mutant exhibited a colonization defect at 7 dpf relative to the wild-type strain.
source: We observed a similar colonization defect at 7 dpf with the Aer ΔAΔB mutant relative to the wild-type strain (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Single gene deletion strains of aimA or aimB colonized to wild-type levels.
source: However, the single gene deletion strains colonized to wild-type levels, suggesting that AimA and AimB provide redundant functions for Aeromonas growth within the larval intestine.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Addition of purified AimA protein at 100 ng/mL completely restored the colonization efficiency of the aim deficient strains.
source: Remarkably, addition of purified AimA protein at a concentration of 100 ng/mL to the flask water from 4 to 7 dpf completely restored the colonization efficiency of the aim deficient strains (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B,C

claim: Zebrafish mono-associated with ZF Aer ΔaimA exhibited significantly higher intestinal neutrophil counts compared with those colonized with wild-type ZF Aer.
source: We found that zebrafish mono-associated with ZF Aer ΔaimA exhibited significantly higher intestinal neutrophil counts as compared with those colonized with wild-type ZF Aer (Figure 5D), despite carrying a lower bacterial load (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5B

claim: Zebrafish colonized with the double mutant Aer ΔAΔB had significantly higher neutrophil counts than fish colonized with wild-type Aer.
source: Similarly, zebrafish colonized with the double mutant, Aer ΔAΔB, had significantly higher neutrophil counts than fish colonized with wild-type Aer (Figure 5E), despite being colonized at a lower level (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5C

claim: The Aer ΔaimA and Aer ΔaimB single mutants did not induce higher intestinal neutrophil numbers.
source: Notably, the Aer ΔaimA and Aer ΔaimB single mutants, which did not exhibit decreased colonization in mono-associations, also did not induce higher intestinal neutrophil numbers (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Exogenous AimA reduced neutrophil numbers back to normal levels in fish mono-associated with inflammation-inducing Δaim strains.
source: For both Aeromonas lineages, when exogenous AimA was added to the flasks of fish mono-associated with inflammation-inducing Δaim strains, the protein reduced neutrophil numbers back to normal levels (Figure 5D,E) and at the same time restored colonization levels (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D,E and Figure 5B,C

claim: Aer ΔAΔB is much more immuno-stimulatory than the wild-type strain, recruiting nearly twice the number of neutrophils per 10^4 colonizing bacteria.
source: By extrapolating the number of neutrophils elicited per 104 colonizing bacteria, we calculated that Aer ΔAΔB is much more immuno-stimulatory that the wild-type strain, recruiting nearly twice the number of neutrophils, on average, for the same number of bacteria (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The survival rate of zebrafish colonized with wild-type Aer was 92% at 72 hr post-inoculation.
source: By 72 hr post-inoculation, the survival rate of zebrafish colonized with wild-type Aer was 92% (n = 163).
evidence: Supported by experimental survival data

claim: Zebrafish mono-associated with Aeromonas lacking Aim genes had significantly reduced survival rates (64%, 73%, and 55% for ΔaimA, ΔaimB, and ΔAΔB, respectively).
source: We observed a significant decline in the survival of fish mono-associated with Aeromonas lacking Aim genes [Aer ΔaimA (n = 139), Aer ΔaimB (n = 174), and Aer ΔAΔB (n = 148)], with survival rates of 64%, 73%, and 55%, respectively (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The decreased survival rate of fish colonized with Aeromonas lacking Aim genes was rescued back to 90% by the presence of purified AimA protein.
source: Remarkably, this decreased survival rate was rescued back to 90% by the presence of purified AimA protein (n = 60; Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Both Aer ΔAΔB and wild-type Aer colonized myd88-/- fish to equivalent levels, which were significantly higher than in wild-type fish.
source: We found that both Aer ΔAΔB and wild-type Aer colonized myd88-/- fish to equivalent levels, which were significantly higher than in wild-type fish (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: The hosts' innate immune response contributes to limiting bacterial colonization.
source: These results suggest that the decreased colonization of Aer ΔAΔB compared to wild-type Aeromonas in wild-type fish is due to the increased inflammatory response to the mutant bacteria, and moreover suggest that the hosts' innate immune response contributes to limiting bacterial colonization.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that bacteria colonize to higher levels in myd88-/- fish

claim: myd88-/- fish inoculated with wild-type Aeromonas or Aer ΔAΔB died at the same rate.
source: We further found that myd88-/- fish inoculated with wild-type Aeromonas or Aer ΔAΔB died at the same rate (Figure 6E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E

claim: The increased inflammatory response of wild-type fish colonized with Aer ΔAΔB compared to wild-type Aeromonas accounts for the decreased fish survival rate with the mutant bacteria.
source: suggesting that the increased inflammatory response of wild-type fish colonized with Aer ΔAΔB compared to wild-type Aeromonas accounts for the decreased fish survival rate with the mutant bacteria.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that survival rates are equal in myd88-/- fish

claim: myd88-/- fish mono-associated with either wild-type or Aer ΔAΔB perished at higher rates than wild type fish.
source: Notably, the myd88-/- fish mono-associated with either wild-type or Aer ΔAΔB perished at higher rates than wild type fish, indicating that there is a host fitness cost to failing to control Aeromonas levels.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E

claim: AimA extended the median survival time of LPS-exposed zebrafish from 32 hr to 47 hr.
source: The median survival time post LPS treatment was 32 hr, which we found was extended to 47 hr in the presence of AimA (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Purified AimB extended the median survival of LPS-exposed zebrafish to 47 hr.
source: Using the same treatment paradigm, we found that purified AimB also extended the median survival of LPS-exposed zebrafish to 47 hr (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Treatment with mLCN2 had no effect on zebrafish survival in LPS intoxication (median survival 34 hr).
source: In contrast, treatment with mLCN2 had no effect on zebrafish survival (median survival 34 hr, Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F

claim: AimA and AimB, but not mLCN2, significantly extend the survival of zebrafish in an LPS intoxication model.
source: Thus, AimA and AimB, but not mLCN2, significantly extend the survival of zebrafish in an LPS intoxication model.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F

claim: AimA is required during bacterial colonization of larval zebrafish to prevent an intestinal inflammatory response that is detrimental to both partners.
source: Here we describe the discovery of AimA, a bacterial immunomodulatory protein secreted by Aeromonas that is required during bacterial colonization of larval zebrafish to prevent an intestinal inflammatory response that is detrimental to both partners.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: AimA consists of two structurally similar lipocalin-like domains.
source: We determined the molecular structure of AimA and show that it consists of two structurally similar lipocalin-like domains, each of which acts to suppress intestinal inflammation.
evidence: Supported by structural determination and functional assays

claim: Each of AimA's subdomains prevents chemically induced intestinal inflammation.
source: We determined the molecular structure of AimA and show that it consists of two structurally similar lipocalin-like domains, each of which acts to suppress intestinal inflammation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: AimA's activity is blocked by exogenous mouse LCN2.
source: Furthermore, we found that this activity is blocked by exogenous mouse LCN2 (mLCN2), implying a shared mechanism of action between these structurally similar bacterial and mammalian proteins.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: AimA does not appear to function like LCN2 as a binding protein for bacterial siderophores.
source: However, AimA does not appear to function like LCN2 as a binding protein for bacterial siderophores.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G

claim: In mono-associations with aim mutants, both the host and bacterial partners suffered reduced viability.
source: In mono-associations with aim mutants, we found that both the host and bacterial partners suffered reduced viability, which could be rescued with exogenous AimA protein.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 6

claim: The fitness cost to the bacteria from lacking aim genes was due to excessive inflammation.
source: We showed that the fitness cost to the bacteria was due to excessive inflammation because the aim mutant survival deficit was erased in an immunocompromised host.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D,E

claim: AimA's benefit to the host extended to protection from lipopolysaccharide intoxication.
source: In parallel, we showed AimA's benefit to the host extended to protection from lipopolysaccharide (LPS) intoxication.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F

claim: All resident bacteria produce microbial associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) that are inherently pro-inflammatory.
source: All resident bacteria produce microbial associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) that are inherently pro-inflammatory, as we have shown in zebrafish larvae for LPS, which elicits intestinal neutrophil influx, proinflammatory cytokine gene expression, and endotoxemia in a dose-dependent manner (Bates et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bates et al., 2007

claim: Few zebrafish microbiota members elicit dose-dependent inflammation.
source: However, our analysis of dose response curves to resident bacteria revealed that few zebrafish microbiota members elicit dose-dependent inflammation (Rolig et al., 2015; Rolig et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rolig et al., 2015; Rolig et al., 2017

claim: The majority of zebrafish gut bacteria showed no correlation between their bacterial load and the number of neutrophils they elicited.
source: However, the majority of zebrafish gut bacteria we surveyed, including Aeromonas species, showed no correlation between their bacterial load and the number of neutrophils they elicited (Rolig et al., 2015; Rolig et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Rolig et al., 2015; Rolig et al., 2017

claim: Most gut bacteria possess both pro-inflammatory products and neutralizing mechanisms to counteract the effects on their hosts.
source: suggesting that most gut bacteria posses both pro-inflammatory products, like LPS, along with neutralizing mechanisms to counteract the effects on their hosts.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that most bacteria don't show dose-dependent inflammation

claim: Lipocalin domains are found across the tree of life.
source: Lipocalin domains are found across the tree of life, with bacterial lipocalin fold-containing proteins being only more recently identified (Bishop, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bishop, 2000

claim: In eukaryotes, proteins with lipocalin folds commonly bind small hydrophobic molecules such as odorant molecules, retinol, and fatty acids.
source: In eukaryotes, proteins with lipocalin folds commonly bind small hydrophobic molecules such as odorant molecules, retinol, and fatty acids (Flower, 1996)
evidence: Supported by citation to Flower, 1996

claim: LCN2 was originally identified and purified from neutrophil granules.
source: LCN2 was originally identified and purified from neutrophil granules and shown to play a critical role in neutrophil extravasation and migration—processes that AimA may also modulate.
evidence: Established knowledge about LCN2

claim: LCN2 is a sensitive fecal biomarker of intestinal inflammation in humans and mice.
source: LCN2 was subsequently shown to be a sensitive fecal biomarker of intestinal inflammation in humans and mice (Chassaing et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chassaing et al., 2012

claim: Lcn2 deficient mice are sensitized to developing colitis.
source: Inflammation-associated induction of LCN2 appears to be protective against pathology because Lcn2 deficient mice are sensitized to developing colitis (Toyonaga et al., 2016; Moschen et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Toyonaga et al., 2016; Moschen et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2016

claim: Lactococcus lactis engineered to overexpress mLCN2 confers greater protection against colitis than a control strain in a mouse model of acute colitis.
source: Further, Lactococcus lactis engineered to overexpress mLCN2 confers greater protection against colitis than a control strain of L. lactis in a mouse model of acute colitis (Saha et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saha et al., 2017

claim: LCN2 binds at least two known mammalian receptors, megalin and LCN2R, which have homologues in zebrafish.
source: LCN2 binds at least two known mammalian receptors, megalin and LCN2R, which have homologues in zebrafish (Kim et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2011

claim: The binding of LCN2 to megalin and LCN2R has not been directly connected to the influence of LCN2 on neutrophil behavior.
source: although the binding to these receptors has not been directly connected to the influence of LCN2 on neutrophil behavior (Moschen et al., 2017; Cabedo Martinez et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Moschen et al., 2017; Cabedo Martinez et al., 2016

claim: mLCN2 exists both as monomers and as dimers.
source: mLCN2 is known to exist both as monomers and as dimers (Axelsson et al., 1995; Perduca et al., 2001; Niemi et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Axelsson et al., 1995; Perduca et al., 2001; Niemi et al., 2015

claim: The dimeric form of mLCN2 is associated with neutrophils.
source: and while little is known about the conditions under which each form is active, the dimeric form is associated with neutrophils (Cai et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cai et al., 2010

claim: AimA represents a new class of bacterial effector proteins called mutualism factors.
source: In this regard, AimA represents a new class of bacterial effector proteins, which we refer to as mutualism factors.
evidence: Authors' conceptual classification based on experimental findings

claim: A mutualism factor confers mutual benefits, and both partners suffer when it is removed from the host-microbe symbiosis.
source: Whereas virulence factors promote the fitness of pathogens to the detriment of their hosts and are revealed by the decreased fitness of the pathogen mutants coupled to the increased fitness of the host, a mutualism factor like AimA confers mutual benefits, and both partners suffer when it is removed from the host-microbe symbiosis.
evidence: Authors' definition based on experimental observations

claim: Bacteroidetes fragilis PSA induces T regulatory cells that benefit the murine host by preventing excessive inflammation.
source: Another example of a mutualism factor is the zwitterionic polysaccharide PSA produced by Bacteroidetes fragilis, which colonizes the murine colon. PSA induces T regulatory cells (T regs), which benefit its murine host by preventing excessive inflammation.
evidence: Established knowledge about PSA function

claim: T regulatory cells contribute to B. fragilis colonization.
source: The T regs in turn contribute to B. fragilis colonization, as demonstrated by the fact that in the absence of T regs, due either to genetic ablation or absence of PSA-induction, B. fragilis suffers a colonization defect (Round et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Round et al., 2011

claim: Intestinal microbiota are rich sources of novel anti-inflammatory factors that enable resident microbes to colonize at high density without eliciting excessive inflammation.
source: Given the constraints of bacterial-host coexistence in the vertebrate intestine, we speculate that intestinal microbiota are rich sources of novel anti-inflammatory factors that enable resident microbes to colonize this tissue at high density without eliciting excessive inflammation.
evidence: Speculative statement based on study findings

claim: The high throughput gnotobiotic larval zebrafish system provides an experimentally tractable platform for discovery of anti-inflammatory factors.
source: Such anti-inflammatory factors offer promise for useful therapeutic applications, and the high throughput gnotobiotic larval zebrafish system provides an experimentally tractable platform for their discovery.
evidence: Authors' assessment based on their experimental approach

claim: AimA and LCN2 may have overlapping functions as mutualism factors in the vertebrate intestine even though they are provisioned by different members of the partnership.
source: Our discovery of AimA raises the possibility that AimA and LCN2 have overlapping functions as mutualism factors in the vertebrate intestine even though they are provisioned by different members of the partnership.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of findings

claim: AimA is likely only the first of many unique bacterial proteins that facilitate mutualistic interactions critical for both host and resident microbes to thrive.
source: Given the diversity of the microbial communities that are part of the complex host-microbe ecosystem, AimA is likely only the first of many unique bacterial proteins that facilitate mutualistic interactions critical for both host and resident microbes to thrive.
evidence: Speculative statement based on study findings

claim: The ΔT2C and ΔT2 strains colonized the zebrafish intestine to similar levels in mono-associations.
source: The ΔT2C and ΔT2 colonized the zebrafish intestine to similar levels in mono-associations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Aer ΔT2 did not exhibit a colonization defect similar to the Aer ΔAΔB mutant.
source: We note that Aer ΔT2 did not exhibit a colonization defect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) similar to the Aer ΔAΔB mutant, which could be due to other phenotypic consequences of its altered secretion profile.
evidence: Observation from experimental data with speculative interpretation

claim: All Aeromonas mutants (ΔaimA, ΔaimB, ΔAΔB, and ZF Aer ΔaimA) displayed normal growth in vitro in rich media.
source: All of these mutants displayed normal growth in vitro in rich media (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Wild type Hm21 and the Aer ΔAΔB mutant had identical growth curves when grown under iron starvation.
source: We found that the two strains had identical growth curves when grown under iron starvation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that AimA and AimB do not function in iron acquisition for Aeromonas.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: AimA and AimB do not function in iron acquisition for Aeromonas.
source: We found that the two strains had identical growth curves when grown under iron starvation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that AimA and AimB do not function in iron acquisition for Aeromonas.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that aim mutants grow normally under iron starvation

claim: myd88-/- mutant fish have a severely attenuated intestinal neutrophil response.
source: For these experiments, we used myd88-/- mutant fish lacking the adaptor protein for inducing many toll-like receptor and IL-1 dependent pro-inflammatory pathways (Larsson et al., 2012); these fish have a severely attenuated intestinal neutrophil response (Figure 6C) that is indistinguishable from GF wild-type zebrafish (Figure 1A), as we have reported previously (Bates et al., 2007; Burns et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and citations to Larsson et al., 2012; Bates et al., 2007; Burns et al., 2017

claim: The intestinal neutrophil response in myd88-/- fish is indistinguishable from GF wild-type zebrafish.
source: these fish have a severely attenuated intestinal neutrophil response (Figure 6C) that is indistinguishable from GF wild-type zebrafish (Figure 1A), as we have reported previously (Bates et al., 2007; Burns et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 1A, with citations to Bates et al., 2007; Burns et al., 2017
